## Linear Independence

**Definition 2.3.2.1** (Linear Independence).  
A set of vectors $\{\mathbf{u_1}, \mathbf{u_2}, \dots, \mathbf{u_k}\} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is said to be **linearly independent** if the only solution to the equation

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_i \mathbf{u_i} = \mathbf{0}
$$

is when all scalars are zero:

$$
\alpha_1 = \alpha_2 = \dots = \alpha_k = 0
$$

That is, no vector in the set can be written as a linear combination of the others. If there exists at least one non-trivial solution (i.e., at least one scalar is non-zero), then the set is said to be **linearly dependent**.

Let each vector be represented in component form as:

$$
\mathbf{u_i} = \begin{bmatrix} u_i(1)\\ u_i(2)\\ \vdots\\ u_i(n) \end{bmatrix}
$$

Then, the linear combination becomes:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_i \mathbf{u_i} = \begin{bmatrix} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_i u_i(1) \\ \sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_i u_i(2) \\ \vdots \\ \sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_i u_i(n) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$

The function that performs this linear check may be written as:

$$
\mathbf{L} : \mathbb{R}^k \times \underbrace{\mathbb{R}^n \times \dots \times \mathbb{R}^n}_{k\text{ times}} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^n \quad \text{such that} \quad \mathbf{L}(\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k, \mathbf{u_1}, \dots, \mathbf{u_k}) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \alpha_i \mathbf{u_i}
$$

---

**Example 2.3.2.1**  
Let $\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$.

We ask: Are $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ linearly independent?

Suppose we try to solve:

$$
\alpha \mathbf{u} + \beta \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
$$

$$
\Rightarrow \alpha \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2 \end{bmatrix} + \beta \begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Expanding:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} \alpha + 2\beta \\ 2\alpha + 4\beta \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Solving:

$$
\begin{cases}
\alpha + 2\beta = 0\\
2\alpha + 4\beta = 0
\end{cases}
$$

This system has infinitely many solutions, such as $\alpha = -2$, $\beta = 1$.  
Hence, the set $\{\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}\}$ is **linearly dependent**.

---

**Example 2.3.2.2**  
Let $\mathbf{a} = \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

Suppose:

$$
\alpha \mathbf{a} + \beta \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}
\Rightarrow 
\begin{bmatrix} \alpha \\ \beta \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Here, the only solution is $\alpha = \beta = 0$.  
Therefore, the set $\{\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}\}$ is **linearly independent**.
